title: Wildlife Laws and Projects in India

cards.h: Law plus projects equals half the topic
cards.b:
UPSC asks both: what the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 does, and what each project achieved. Cheetah, tiger, elephant and dolphin projects are in the news every year.

This lesson also uses current facts. Numbers change, so the year is marked.

Expect the Act in Prelims through its sections, schedules and bodies, and the projects in Mains through a success versus gaps argument. Project Tiger began in 1973, Project Elephant in 1992, and the Gangetic dolphin received a project in later years. Remember to link each project with the nodal agency and the law that gives it legal force.

The Act came after the 1972 Stockholm conference. It bans hunting (Section 9), creates protected areas, sets up Wildlife Advisory Boards, and gives schedules of protected species. Penalties are in Section 51.

India adopted a Constitutional base in 1976 (42nd Amendment): forests and wild animals moved to the Concurrent List (Entries 17A and 17B), and Article 48A and 51A(g) were added.

The Act created schedules of species. Schedule I and Part II of Schedule II carry the highest protection and heaviest penalties. After the 2022 amendment the Act has four schedules, with a new one for CITES-listed specimens, and the old vermin schedule was dropped. The Chief Wildlife Warden is the key State official. The National Board for Wildlife, chaired by the Prime Minister, advises the Centre.

The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 did these things: it cut the schedules from six to four; it dropped the vermin schedule; it added a schedule for CITES specimens and made the Centre the CITES authority; it gave power to regulate invasive alien species; and it allowed states to reconstitute their Wildlife Advisory Board as a Standing Committee.

It also allows voluntary surrender of captive wild animals and regulates elephant transfer for religious uses.

Critics say the Amendment shifts power to the Centre and weakens oversight of captive elephants. Supporters say it brings India in line with CITES and helps curb invasives.

Enforcement is weaker than the law. The Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (2007) tackles trade, but conviction rates are low.

Project Tiger began in 1973 (Corbett was first). The National Tiger Conservation Authority became statutory in 2006. The 2022 estimate reported at least 3,167 tigers from camera traps and a mean estimate near 3,682, which is about 70 percent of the world’s wild tigers.

The next estimation (sixth cycle) began in 2025–26 and its report is expected in 2027. India has 58 tiger reserves in 18 states (as of 2026).

The cheetah went extinct in India in 1952. Eight Namibian cheetahs were released at Kuno National Park (Madhya Pradesh) on 17 September 2022. Twelve more came from South Africa in 2023. Cubs are now born in India.

As of September 2026, secondary reports count about 52 cheetahs, including around 32 born in India, with a few at Gandhi Sagar sanctuary. Banni (Gujarat) and other sites are being prepared. Botswana is a new source country.

• Project Elephant (1992): corridors and elephant reserves. The 2017 census counted 27,312 elephants. The DNA-based 2021–25 estimate, released in October 2025, counted about 22,446 elephants; it uses a new method, so it is not directly comparable.
  • Project Snow Leopard (2009) and the SECURE Himalaya programme.
  • Project Dolphin (announced 2020) for river and ocean dolphins.
  • Crocodile Conservation Project (1975) and gharial work in the Chambal.
  • Project Lion for Gujarat’s Asiatic lions; the 16th lion census (May 2025) counted 891, up from 674 in 2020.

Cheetah supporters say it restores a grassland predator and funds grasslands. Critics say India lacks enough open space, deaths were high in early years, and money would be better spent on the Great Indian Bustard or caracal.

The Supreme Court monitored the project and asked for more sites. The same question applies to tiger relocation: how many animals can the land hold?

Related laws: Forest Conservation Act 1980 (now renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam after the 2023 amendment), Forest Rights Act 2006, Biological Diversity Act 2002 and the Environment Protection Act 1986.

The Supreme Court’s M.K. Ranjitsinh v Union of India (2024) case, on the Great Indian Bustard, recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21.

Mains-style: “Evaluate the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022. Does it strengthen conservation?” Structure: key changes; positives (CITES, invasives, rationalised schedules); negatives (centralisation, captive animals, enforcement); way forward.

Mains-style: “Project Cheetah: success or experiment? Discuss.”

Prelims tip: The 2022 Act cut schedules from six to four. Kuno is in Madhya Pradesh. NTCA is statutory since 2006.

quiz.q: The Wildlife (Protection) Act was passed in:
The 2022 Amendment reduced the number of Schedules from:
quiz.w: It dropped vermin and added a CITES schedule.

quiz.q: Project Cheetah’s first release site was:
quiz.w: Namibian cheetahs were released at Kuno in September 2022.
Corbett National Park was the first reserve.

quiz.q: NTCA became a statutory body in:
quiz.w: The 2006 amendment gave it legal status.

quiz.q: Hunting is prohibited under which Section of the WPA?
quiz.w: Section 9 bans hunting; Section 51 is penalties.
